intro: Jada's morning, told in ten flat sentences, sounds like a robot counting. Told in two, it sounds like a girl running for the bell. A text that says Let's eat Grandma makes a family laugh; a comma turns it back into dinner. In both cases the words were fine. What was missing was the shape around them: the joins, the stops, the small marks that tell a reader how the words go together.

This unit is about that shape. The first chapter takes a sentence apart and puts it back together: phrases and clauses, the four kinds of sentences, how to combine short ones and repair broken ones, and the choices inside a sentence, such as who does the action, what mood the verb takes, which pronoun fits, and where a description attaches. The second chapter turns to the marks and the words: commas, semicolons, colons, dashes, apostrophes, quotation marks, capitals, the words that sound alike, the spelling patterns, and the guides that settle the arguments.

By the end you will be able to name any sentence by counting its clauses, fix a fragment or a run-on four different ways, tell its from it's and affect from effect in one second, and explain why one comma can change who is insulting whom. None of it is about sounding fancy. All of it is about being understood the first time.
bigQuestion: How do the joins inside a sentence and the marks around it control what a reader understands?

timeline.t: You find the subject and the verb in every sentence of a draft, and mark the word groups that have neither.
You label each clause independent or dependent, and circle the word that makes it lean.
You name every sentence by counting clauses: simple, compound, complex or compound-complex.
You combine three short sentences into one, then follow one long sentence with one of five words.
You hunt fragments and run-ons in a paragraph and fix each one a different way.
You turn passive verbs active where the doer matters, and test every I or me by taking the partner out.
You place commas: between items in a series, after openers, and around extra information.
You add one semicolon, one colon and one dash, each where it earns its place.
You check every apostrophe, every quotation mark and every capital letter against its rule.
You read the whole piece aloud, test each look-alike word, choose one style and keep it to the end.

words.d: a group of words with a subject and a verb
a clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
a clause that begins with a word like because or when and cannot stand alone
two or more independent clauses joined by a comma and a conjunction, or by a semicolon
an independent clause joined with at least one dependent clause
a piece of a sentence punctuated as if it were whole
two or more independent clauses jammed together without a proper stop
a sentence form in which the subject receives the action instead of doing it
the verb mood for wishes, demands and things contrary to fact: If I were you
the noun a pronoun stands in for
describes a clause that only adds information and is set off with commas
the mark that shows possession or stands in for missing letters, never a plural

test.q: Which group of words is a clause?
test.why: The crowd cheered has a subject and a verb. The other three are phrases.

choices: The bell rang, and we left.
Because the bell rang, we left.
test.why: Because the bell rang is a dependent clause attached to an independent clause. That makes a complex sentence.
Because leaves the thought hanging, and nothing completes it.
Two independent clauses held apart by only a comma make a comma splice.

test.q: Which sentence is in active voice?
choices: The fort was built by the kids.
The fort was built in a day.
test.why: The kids, the subject, do the building. In the others the fort receives the action.

test.q: Which sentence is in the imperative mood?
choices: If you rested, you would feel better.
test.why: Rest before the game is a command with the subject you left out.
Both pronouns are subjects, so both take subject case: she and I.

test.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
choices: While waiting for the bus, I read.
I read while I waited for the bus.
While I waited, the bus never came.
While waiting for the bus, the book got wet.
test.why: The book was not waiting for the bus. The opening phrase has no doer next to it.

choices: We need paper, tape, and glue.
We need, paper, tape, and glue.
We need paper tape and glue.
We need paper, tape, and, glue.
test.why: Commas separate the items in the series. No comma belongs after need or after and.

test.q: Which sentence means you have more than one uncle?
choices: My uncle, who lives in Rockford, is a chef.
My uncle who lives in Rockford is a chef.
My uncle is a chef in Rockford.
Rockford is where my uncle, a chef, lives.
test.why: Without commas, who lives in Rockford is restrictive: it picks out one uncle from several.

choices: She wanted a bike: and a helmet.
She wanted one thing: a bike.
test.why: She wanted one thing is a complete sentence, so the colon can introduce what follows.
Dogs is a plain plural with no apostrophe, and their shows possession.
The comma links the quote to its tag and sits inside the closing quotation mark.

choices: The cold weather effected the crops.
The cold weather affected the crops.
The cold weather had an affect on the crops.
The cold weather was effecting the crops.
test.why: Affect is the verb: the weather changed the crops. Effect is the noun.
Stop is a short word with one vowel, so the p doubles before -ing to keep the o short.

write.prompt: Make a claim: which single rule from this unit, about sentences or about punctuation, matters most for a reader? Support it with two examples from the unit where breaking that rule changed the meaning, and explain how those examples prove your claim.
tips: State your claim in one sentence, naming the rule: for example, the comma around extra information, or fixing run-ons.
Use two examples from the lessons, such as the Peoria brother, Let's eat Grandma, or the backpack that ran for the bus. Show the sentence with the error and without it.
For each example, explain what a reader would understand wrongly if the rule were broken. That explanation is your reasoning.
Give the other side one sentence: name a different rule someone might pick, and say why yours matters more.
Check your own draft against your rule before you turn it in.
